claim: The brain actively reshapes our understanding of past events in light of new incoming information.
source: The brain actively reshapes our understanding of past events in light of new incoming information.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that frames the study's motivation.

claim: One group of participants watched a movie ('The Sixth Sense') with a cinematic 'twist' at the end that dramatically changed the interpretation of previous events.
source: One group of participants watched a movie ('The Sixth Sense') with a cinematic 'twist' at the end that dramatically changed the interpretation of previous events.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and stimulus used in the study.

claim: Participants were asked to verbally recall the movie events, taking into account the new 'twist' information.
source: Next, participants were asked to verbally recall the movie events, taking into account the new 'twist' information.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: Most participants updated their recall to incorporate the twist.
source: Most participants updated their recall to incorporate the twist.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: Two additional groups recalled the movie without having to update their memories during recall: one group never saw the twist; another group was exposed to the twist prior to the beginning of the movie.
source: Two additional groups recalled the movie without having to update their memories during recall: one group never saw the twist; another group was exposed to the twist prior to the beginning of the movie, and thus the twist information was incorporated both during encoding and recall.
evidence: This describes the control groups in the experimental design.

claim: Providing participants with information about the twist beforehand altered neural response patterns during movie-viewing in the default mode network (DMN).
source: We found that providing participants with information about the twist beforehand altered neural response patterns during movie-viewing in the default mode network (DMN).
evidence: This is a main neural finding from the study.

claim: Presenting participants with the twist at the end of the movie changed the neural representation of the previously-encoded information during recall in a subset of DMN regions.
source: Moreover, presenting participants with the twist at the end of the movie changed the neural representation of the previously-encoded information during recall in a subset of DMN regions.
evidence: This is a main neural finding from the study.

claim: Neural representations of past events encoded in the DMN are dynamically integrated with new information that reshapes our understanding in natural contexts.
source: Our results demonstrate that neural representations of past events encoded in the DMN are dynamically integrated with new information that reshapes our understanding in natural contexts.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Memories are malleable to modification when they are reactivated and relevant new information is presented.
source: Research in the last few decades suggests that memories are malleable to modification when they are reactivated (Przybyslawski and Sara, 1997), and relevant new information is presented (Besnard et al., 2012; Hupbach et al., 2015; Nader and Einarsson, 2010; Sinclair and Barense, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DMN was originally described as an intrinsic or 'task-negative' network, activated when participants are not engaged with external stimuli.
source: The brain's default mode network (DMN)—comprising the posterior medial cortex, medial prefrontal cortex, temporoparietal junction, and parts of anterior temporal cortex—was originally described as an intrinsic or 'task-negative' network, activated when participants are not engaged with external stimuli (Raichle et al., 2001; Buckner et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DMN is an important hub for supporting internally driven tasks such as memory retrieval, imagination, future planning, theory of mind, and creating and updating situation models.
source: This observation led to a large body of work showing that the DMN is an important hub for supporting internally driven tasks such as memory retrieval, imagination, future planning, theory of mind, and creating and updating situation models (Svoboda et al., 2006; Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Hassabis and Maguire, 2009; Schacter and Addis, 2007; Szpunar et al., 2007; Spreng et al., 2009; Koster-Hale and Saxe, 2013; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DMN is reliably engaged during 'online' processing (encoding) of continuous rich dynamic stimuli such as movies and audio stories.
source: Interestingly, prior work has also shown that the DMN is reliably engaged during 'online' processing (encoding) of continuous rich dynamic stimuli such as movies and audio stories (Stephens et al., 2013; Hasson et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Regions in the DMN have long 'temporal receptive windows', meaning that they integrate and retain high-level information that accumulates over the course of extended timescales.
source: Regions in this network have been shown to have long 'temporal receptive windows' (Hasson et al., 2008; Lerner et al., 2011; Chang et al., 2022), meaning that they integrate and retain high-level information that accumulates over the course of extended timescales (e.g. scenes in movies, paragraphs in text) to support comprehension.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Neural patterns during encoding and recall of naturalistic stimuli (movies) are reliably similar across participants in the DMN.
source: Recent work has shown that neural patterns during encoding and recall of naturalistic stimuli (movies) are reliably similar across participants in this network (Chen et al., 2017; Oedekoven et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017; see Bird, 2020 for a review of recent naturalistic studies on memory), and the DMN displays distinct neural activity when listening to the same story with different perspectives (Yeshurun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The movie 'The Sixth Sense' depicts the story of a clinical psychologist treating a child who claims to see ghosts.
source: The movie depicts the story of a clinical psychologist treating a child who claims to see ghosts.
evidence: This describes the content of the stimulus used in the study.

claim: In the final scene of 'The Sixth Sense', it is revealed that the doctor was in fact, a ghost himself throughout the movie.
source: In the final scene, it is revealed that the doctor was in fact, a ghost himself throughout the movie.
evidence: This describes the content of the stimulus used in the study.

claim: There are two coherent interpretations of the movie: the Doctor (or naive) interpretation and the Ghost (or spoiled) interpretation.
source: Therefore, there are two coherent interpretations of the movie: the Doctor (or naive) interpretation (labeled D in Figure 1), which is typically held by viewers up until they encounter the 'twist ending'; and the Ghost (or spoiled) interpretation (labeled G in Figure 1), which is held by viewers after they learn about the twist.
evidence: This describes the conceptual framework of the study.

claim: Memory updating is operationalized as the transition from the Doctor (D) interpretation to the Ghost (G) interpretation.
source: In this setting, memory updating is operationalized as the transition from the Doctor (D) interpretation to the Ghost (G) interpretation.
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the study.

claim: Participants who received the twist and are aware that the doctor is a ghost might have distinct neural representations of the events from those who encoded the movie while ignorant of the twist.
source: Our study design hinges on the hypothesis that participants who received the twist and are aware that the doctor is a ghost might have distinct neural representations of the events from those who encoded the movie while ignorant of the twist.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: Encountering the twist after encoding the movie would initiate a retrospective update in the interpretation of the encoded movie and that this update would be reflected in both verbal recall and patterns of brain activity during remembering.
source: Importantly, we predicted that encountering the twist after encoding the movie would initiate a retrospective update in the interpretation of the encoded movie and that this update would be reflected in both verbal recall and patterns of brain activity during remembering.
evidence: This is a prediction of the study.

claim: The neural representations of the events in the movie will remain unchanged during recall in subjects who do not need to update their memories during recall.
source: In contrast, the neural representations of the events in the movie will remain unchanged during recall in subjects who do not need to update their memories during recall (i.e. in subjects in the 'no-twist' condition who are only aware of the D interpretation, or subjects in the 'spoiler' condition who knew all along about the G interpretation).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study.

claim: In a large set of regions in the DMN, context changed how the movie was encoded into memory.
source: In a large set of regions in the DMN, we found that context changed how the movie was encoded into memory.
evidence: This is a main finding from the study.

claim: The neural representations for each event in the movie were different for viewers who believed the doctor was alive versus viewers who believed the doctor was a ghost.
source: In other words, the neural representations for each event in the movie were different for viewers who believed the doctor was alive versus viewers who believed the doctor was a ghost.
evidence: This is a main finding from the study.

claim: In several DMN regions, neural representations were updated during recall for viewers who learned that the doctor was a ghost after watching the movie.
source: Furthermore, in several DMN regions, we found that neural representations were updated during recall for viewers who learned that the doctor was a ghost after watching the movie.
evidence: This is a main finding from the study.

claim: Areas in the default mode network are actively updating the neural representations as they integrate incoming information with prior knowledge.
source: Together these results suggest that areas in the default mode network are actively updating the neural representations as they integrate incoming information with prior knowledge.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Three distinct experimental groups watched concise versions of 'The Sixth Sense' in the fMRI scanner.
source: Three distinct experimental groups watched concise versions of a popular Hollywood-style film titled "The Sixth Sense" (M. Night Shyamalan, 1999) in the fMRI scanner (Figure 1B, left column).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Following the movie viewing all three groups were asked to freely recall the movie in the scanner.
source: Following the movie viewing all three groups were asked to freely recall the movie in the scanner (Figure 1B, left column).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Participants in the 'twist' condition watched the movie naive to the true nature of the doctor (Movie-Doctor or MD).
source: Participants in the main group (the 'twist' condition, Figure 1B, middle row), watched the movie with the twist scene at the end. Therefore, they watched the movie naive to the true nature of the doctor (Movie-Doctor or MD).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: During recall, participants in the 'twist' condition were aware of the twist information and could use it to update their memory (Recall-Ghost or RG).
source: During their recall, however, they were aware of the twist information and could use it to update their memory (Recall-Ghost or RG).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Participants in the 'spoiled' condition were exposed to the twist at the beginning of the movie.
source: Therefore, we introduced two other groups to the study: participants in one group (the 'spoiled' condition; Figure 1B, top row) were exposed to the twist at the beginning of the movie.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 'spoiled' group watched and recalled the movie knowing that the doctor was a ghost (MG and RG).
source: This group watched and recalled the movie knowing that the doctor was a ghost (MG and RG).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 'no-twist' group never received the twist information throughout encoding and remained naive to the true nature of the doctor in both their encoding and recall (MD and RD).
source: The other group (the 'no-twist' condition; Figure 1B, bottom row) never received the twist information throughout encoding and remained naive to the true nature of the doctor in both their encoding and recall (MD and RD).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The 'twist' group would be more similar to the 'no-twist' group during encoding (both having the Doctor interpretation) but more similar to the 'spoiled' group during recall (both having the Ghost interpretation).
source: We predicted that the 'twist' group would be more similar to the 'no-twist' group during encoding (both having the Doctor interpretation) but more similar to the 'spoiled' group during recall (both having the Ghost interpretation).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study.

claim: Intersubject pattern similarity analysis (intersubject pattern correlation: pISC) was used to compare the neural event representations between groups.
source: We used intersubject pattern similarity analysis (intersubject pattern correlation: pISC, see Methods) to compare the neural event representations between groups.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used in the study.

claim: pISC captures scene-specific pattern similarity between groups who watched the same movie, groups who verbally recalled the same story, and across viewing and recall of the same scenes.
source: This analytic approach is motivated by prior work showing that slowly-evolving activity patterns in DMN represent event-level information (Baldassano et al., 2018) and that pISC captures scene-specific pattern similarity between groups who watched the same movie, groups who verbally recalled the same story (in their own words), and across viewing and recall of the same scenes (Chen et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Scene-specific neural patterns during encoding of the movie were obtained by averaging data across time within each scene in each subject.
source: In this analysis, scene-specific neural patterns during encoding of the movie were obtained by averaging data across time within each scene in each subject (Chen et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the analysis method used in the study.

claim: For the cued recall data, a GLM analysis was run to capture responses corresponding to the recall of single events.
source: For the cued recall data, we ran a GLM analysis (Mumford et al., 2012) to capture responses corresponding to the recall of single events.
evidence: This describes the analysis method used in the study.

claim: The analyses focused on a predetermined selection of 7 'critical scenes' out of 18 total scenes in which the Doctor or Ghost interpretation of the main character would dramatically change the overall interpretation of those scenes.
source: We focused our analyses on a predetermined selection of movie scenes (i.e. 7 'critical scenes' out of 18 total scenes) in which the Doctor or Ghost interpretation of the main character in the movie would dramatically change the overall interpretation of those scenes.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: Selection of critical scenes was based on ratings from five raters asked to quantify the influence of the twist on the interpretation of each scene.
source: Selection of these scenes was based on ratings from five raters asked to quantify the influence of the twist on the interpretation of each scene (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the method for selecting critical scenes.

claim: Participants were highly accurate in recognizing the corresponding scenes from the movie cues (94% accuracy in the 'twist' group, 93% in the 'spoiled' group, and 97% in the 'no-twist' group).
source: Participants were highly accurate in recognizing the corresponding scenes from the movie cues (94% accuracy in the 'twist' group, 93% in the 'spoiled' group, and 97% in the 'no-twist'group).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: Only the scenes that were correctly recalled were included in the neural analyses.
source: Only the scenes that were correctly recalled were included in the neural analyses.
evidence: This describes the data inclusion criteria.

claim: Memory score assessed the quality and detail of memory.
source: Memory score assessed the quality and detail of memory.
evidence: This describes a behavioral measure used in the study.

claim: Twist score assessed whether the twist information was incorporated into the recall and ranged from 1 (the recall purely reflected the Doctor interpretation) to 5 (the recall purely reflected the Ghost interpretation).
source: Twist score assessed whether the twist information was incorporated into the recall and ranged from 1 (the recall purely reflected the Doctor interpretation) to 5 (the recall purely reflected the Ghost interpretation).
evidence: This describes a behavioral measure used in the study.

claim: There was no significant correlation between memory scores and twist scores across participants (r=0.07, p=0.56).
source: Indeed, there was no significant correlation between memory scores and twist scores across participants (r=0.07, p=0.56).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: In the 'twist' group, 14 out of 19 participants scored above 2 on the twist score, indicating that they incorporated the new interpretation into their recall.
source: In the main experimental group ('twist' group), 14 out of 19 participants scored above 2 (median score = 3.25) on the twist score, indicating that they incorporated the new interpretation into their recall.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: The 'twist' group (twist score: M=3.16, SD = 1.03) exhibited a significantly higher twist score (t(37) = 6.37, p<0.001) than the 'no-twist' group (twist score: M=1.65, SD = 0.22).
source: Importantly, the 'twist' group (twist score: M=3.16, SD = 1.03) exhibited a significantly higher twist score (t(37) = 6.37, p<0.001) than the 'no-twist' group (twist score: M=1.65, SD = 0.22).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: Participants in the 'twist group' updated their memories of the movie to incorporate the twist.
source: Therefore, this result confirms that participants in the 'twist group' updated their memories of the movie to incorporate the twist.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: No significant difference (t(35) = 1.46, p=0.15) was observed between the twist score of the 'twist' group and the 'spoiled' group (twist score: M=2.72, SD = 0.74).
source: No significant difference (t(35) = 1.46, p=0.15) was observed between the twist score of the 'twist' group and the 'spoiled' group (twist score: M=2.72, SD = 0.74).
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: The 'twist' group recalled the movie more similarly to the group that knew the twist while watching the movie.
source: This finding suggests that the 'twist' group recalled the movie more similarly to the group that knew the twist while watching the movie.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Most participants in the 'twist' condition talked about both interpretations of the movie scenes in many of the recalled scenes.
source: A surprising observation during the analysis of the behavioral recall in the 'twist' condition was that most participants talked about both interpretations of the movie scenes in many of the recalled scenes (this pattern was observed in the recall of the 'spoiled' group as well).
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the study.

claim: Participants kept both interpretations in mind during the recall, instead of overwriting the Doctor representation with the Ghost representation.
source: Thus, it appeared that participants kept both interpretations in mind during the recall, instead of overwriting the Doctor representation with the Ghost representation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Recalls were typically structured as, 'Initially I thought that… but now I know that…'.
source: These recalls were typically structured as, "Initially I thought that… but now I know that…".
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the study.

claim: Some instances of this recall behavior were also observed in the 'spoiled' group, who had watched the movie knowing the doctor is a ghost.
source: Interestingly, some instances of this recall behavior were also observed in the 'spoiled' group, who had watched the movie knowing the doctor is a ghost (e.g. "You could think that… but I knew that…").
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the study.

claim: The neural representations supporting recall in the 'twist' and 'spoiled' groups included both the original (Doctor) and updated (Ghost) interpretations.
source: This suggests that the neural representations supporting recall in the 'twist' and 'spoiled' groups included both the original (Doctor) and updated (Ghost) interpretations, which could make differentiating these representations in the neural analysis more challenging (see Discussion).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: Within the regions of the brain that are sensitive to different interpretations, the pattern similarity between the 'twist' group (MD) and the 'no-twist' group (MD) should be higher than the similarity between the 'twist' group (MD) and the 'spoiled' group (MG).
source: We hypothesized that within the regions of the brain that are sensitive to different interpretations, the pattern similarity between the 'twist' group (MD) and the 'no-twist' group (MD) should be higher than the similarity between the 'twist' group (MD) and the 'spoiled' group (MG) (Figure 2A, prediction legends).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was significantly greater intersubject pattern correlation in parts of the DMN between the 'twist' and 'no-twist' experimental groups than across experimental groups with opposing interpretations (MD versus MG).
source: Indeed, there was significantly greater intersubject pattern correlation in parts of the DMN between the 'twist' and 'no-twist' experimental groups (who had a similar MD interpretation of the movie during encoding) than across experimental groups with opposing interpretations (MD versus MG).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Areas with significantly greater intersubject pattern correlation between groups who encoded the movie with the same interpretation (Doctor) included the dorsal and lateral PFC, left precuneus, left retrosplenial cortex, left angular gyrus, middle temporal cortex, left superior temporal cortex, and left temporal pole.
source: These areas included the dorsal and lateral PFC, left precuneus, left retrosplenial cortex, left angular gyrus, middle temporal cortex, left superior temporal cortex, and left temporal pole (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: These results fit with previous findings demonstrating that the timecourse of brain responses in DMN regions reflects different perspectives when listening to a spoken narrative.
source: These results fit with previous findings demonstrating that the timecourse of brain responses in DMN regions reflects different perspectives when listening to a spoken narrative (Yeshurun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results extend previous findings by showing that different interpretations are discriminable in spatial response patterns measured while viewing audiovisual movie stimuli.
source: Our results extend these findings by showing that different interpretations are discriminable in spatial response patterns measured while viewing audiovisual movie stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Regions in DMN exhibit different patterns of neural response to Ghost vs. Doctor interpretations.
source: Results from the encoding phase suggest that regions in DMN exhibit different patterns of neural response to Ghost vs. Doctor interpretations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the encoding phase results.

claim: Memory updating is defined as a shift during recall from the neural patterns associated with the Doctor interpretation to incorporate information associated with Ghost interpretation.
source: In the next step, we sought to measure memory updating, which we define as a shift during recall from the neural patterns associated with the Doctor interpretation to incorporate information associated with Ghost interpretation.
evidence: This is the operational definition of memory updating used in the study.

claim: The analysis of recall behavior suggests that participants in the 'twist' condition utilized the twist information to update their recall of the movie.
source: As described earlier, the analysis of recall behavior suggests that participants in the 'twist' condition utilized the twist information to update their recall of the movie.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: During recall, the neural patterns for the 'twist' group might shift from being more similar to the 'no-twist' group as observed during encoding to be more similar to the neural patterns in the 'spoiled' group during recall.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that, during recall, the neural patterns for the 'twist' group might shift from being more similar to the 'no-twist' group as observed during encoding to be more similar to the neural patterns in the 'spoiled' group during recall (Figure 2B – prediction legends).
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: As subjects recalled the movie in the scanner, there was significantly greater intersubject pattern correlation in parts of the DMN between the 'twist' and 'spoiled' experimental groups than across the 'twist' and 'no-twist' groups.
source: Indeed, as subjects recalled the movie in the scanner, there was significantly greater intersubject pattern correlation in parts of the DMN between the 'twist' and 'spoiled' experimental groups (who believed that the doctor is a ghost: RG) than across the 'twist' and 'no-twist' groups (who had opposing interpretations: RG versus RD).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Areas with significantly greater intersubject pattern correlation between groups who recalled the movie with the same interpretation (Ghost) included the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), right precuneus, and right superior temporal cortex.
source: These areas included the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), right precuneus, and right superior temporal cortex (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An interaction analysis highlights a large set of DMN regions where neural patterns in the 'twist' group were relatively more similar to the Ghost (vs. Doctor) interpretation at recall than at encoding.
source: In addition, we ran an interaction analysis to further emphasize the reversal of neural similarity during encoding and recall (see Methods). This analysis highlights a large set of DMN regions, including medial, dorsal, and lateral PFC, precuneus, left retrosplenial cortex, angular gyrus, right superior and middle temporal cortex, and left temporal pole, where neural patterns in the 'twist' group were relatively more similar to the Ghost (vs. Doctor) interpretation at recall than at encoding (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A univariate analysis in each ROI revealed no significant effect of group ('spoiled', 'twist', 'no-twist') or interaction between group and condition (movie, recall).
source: To test whether our reported results were mainly driven by the similarities and differences in multivariate spatial patterns of neural representations, as opposed to by univariate regional-average response magnitudes, we ran a univariate analysis in each ROI. This analysis revealed no significant effect of group ('spoiled', 'twist', 'no-twist') or interaction between group and condition (movie, recall) (Appendix 1—table 1, see Methods for details).
evidence: This is a control analysis finding from the study.

claim: Chen et al., 2017 have demonstrated that, across free recall of a movie, neural patterns are reinstated in DMN.
source: Chen et al., 2017 have demonstrated that, across free recall of a movie, neural patterns are reinstated in DMN.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Scene-specific neural patterns changed between encoding and recall in a systematic manner across individuals.
source: In addition, these scene-specific neural patterns changed between encoding and recall in a systematic manner across individuals (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Updating one's interpretation to incorporate twist information might alter the neural representations during recall, such that they become more similar to the neural patterns elicited during encoding of the spoiled movie.
source: We hypothesized that updating one's interpretation to incorporate twist information might alter the neural representations during recall, such that they become more similar to the neural patterns elicited during encoding of the spoiled movie.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: The neural pattern similarity between recall in the 'twist' group and encoding in the 'spoiled' group (RG to MG) would be higher than the pattern similarity between recall in the 'no-twist' group and encoding of the 'spoiled' group (RD to MG).
source: First, we predicted that (Figure 3A, prediction legend) the neural pattern similarity between recall in the 'twist' group and encoding in the 'spoiled' group (RG to MG) would be higher than the pattern similarity between recall in the 'no-twist' group and encoding of the 'spoiled' group (RD to MG).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The analysis confirmed the prediction that neural pattern similarity between recall in the 'twist' group and encoding in the 'spoiled' group would be higher than the pattern similarity between recall in the 'no-twist' group and encoding of the 'spoiled' group in the left angular gyrus, left dorsomedial PFC, and right middle temporal cortex.
source: Our analysis confirmed this prediction in the left angular gyrus, left dorsomedial PFC, and right middle temporal cortex (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: If participants in the 'twist' group were to fully update their interpretation at recall from Doctor to Ghost, activity patterns during recall in the 'twist' group would be more similar to encoding in the 'spoiled' group (RG to MG) compared to encoding in their own ('twist') group (RG to MD).
source: Second, if participants in the 'twist' group were to fully update their interpretation at recall from Doctor to Ghost, we would expect activity patterns during recall in the 'twist' group to be more similar to encoding in the 'spoiled' group (RG to MG) compared to encoding in their own ('twist') group (RG to MD) (Figure 3B, prediction legends).
evidence: This is a prediction of the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Weak effects in the predicted direction were found in the left angular gyrus, left frontal pole, and right anterior temporal ROIs; however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons at an FDR-corrected p<0.05.
source: When we looked for regions showing this effect, we found weak effects in the predicted direction in the left angular gyrus, left frontal pole, and right anterior temporal ROIs (note that all of these comparisons were performed across participants; see Methods for details); however, these effects did not survive correction for multiple comparisons at an FDR-corrected p<0.05 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The most straightforward interpretation of these weak effects is that, in general, 'twist' group participants did not fully update their interpretations.
source: The most straightforward interpretation of these weak effects is, in general, 'twist' group participants did not fully update their interpretations; that is, there may have been some lingering memory of the Doctor interpretation in the 'twist' group in some participants even after they were exposed to Ghost interpretation and updated their memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural findings.

claim: An exploratory analysis correlated neural pattern change with behavioral twist scores across participants in the 'twist' group, in each DMN ROI.
source: To test this hypothesis, we ran an exploratory analysis where we correlated neural pattern change (i.e. the degree to which the neural pattern at recall matched the Doctor or Ghost encoding pattern) with behavioral twist scores (i.e. how much each subject discussed the twist during recall) across participants in the 'twist' group, in each DMN ROI (Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This describes an exploratory analysis performed in the study.

claim: A positive correlation between neural pattern change and behavioral twist scores was observed in posterior regions of the DMN, including precuneus and angular gyrus.
source: We observed a positive correlation between the neural and behavioral indices of memory update in posterior regions of the DMN, including precuneus and angular gyrus.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory analysis.

claim: The right precuneus ROI exhibited a notable relationship (r=0.62); however, this did not survive FDR correction across ROIs.
source: The right precuneus ROI exhibited a notable relationship (r=0.62); however, this did not survive FDR correction across ROIs.
evidence: This is a finding from the exploratory analysis.

claim: Critical scenes were selected based on ratings from five raters who quantified the influence of the twist on the interpretation of each scene.
source: In the prior analyses, we focused on 'critical scenes', selected based on ratings from five raters who quantified the influence of the twist on the interpretation of each scene (see Methods).
evidence: This describes the method for selecting critical scenes.

claim: An independent post-experiment analysis of the verbal recall behavior of the fMRI participants yielded 'twist scores' that were also highest for these scenes.
source: An independent post-experiment analysis of the verbal recall behavior of the fMRI participants yielded 'twist scores' that were also highest for these scenes; that is, the expected and perceived effect of twist information on recall behavior were found to match.
evidence: This is a behavioral finding from the study.

claim: Critical scenes yielded higher interaction indices compared to all scenes or non-critical scenes across all ROIs.
source: Figure 4A demonstrates that 'critical scenes' yielded higher interaction indices compared to all scenes or non-critical scenes across all ROIs.
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The interaction score across all DMN ROIs was significantly higher in 'critical scenes' than all scenes (t(23) = 7.19, p=2.53 x 10–7) and non-critical scenes (t(23) = 7.3, p=1.95 x 10–7).
source: The interaction score across all DMN ROIs was significantly higher in 'critical scenes' than all scenes (t(23) = 7.19, p=2.53 x 10–7) and non-critical scenes (t(23) = 7.3, p=1.95 x 10–7).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study.

claim: Critical scenes are responsible for the observed pISC differences across groups.
source: These results show that critical scenes are indeed responsible for the observed pISC differences across groups.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scene content analysis.

claim: In 12 out of 24 DMN regions, interaction indices were statistically significant based on the shuffled-scene distribution (p<0.025, FDR controlled at q<.05).
source: In 12 out of 24 DMN regions, interaction indices were statistically significant based on the shuffled-scene distribution (p<0.025, FDR controlled at q<.05).
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The findings from the scene-shuffling analysis confirm that the results are driven by changes to scene-specific representations.
source: Overall, the findings from this analysis confirm that our results are driven by changes to scene-specific representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the scene-shuffling analysis.

claim: The core analyses were focused on regions of the default mode network.
source: We focused our core analyses on regions of the default mode network.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: Prior work has shown that multimodal neural representations of naturalistic events are similar across encoding and verbal recall of the same events in the DMN.
source: Prior work has shown that multimodal neural representations of naturalistic events (e.g. movie scenes) are similar across encoding (movie-watching or story-listening) and verbal recall of the same events in the DMN (Chen et al., 2017; Zadbood et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Retrospective changes in the neural representations of events as the narrative interpretation shifts would be observed in the DMN.
source: Therefore, in the current work we hypothesized that retrospective changes in the neural representations of events as the narrative interpretation shifts would be observed in the DMN.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: The same set of analyses performed in the DMN were run in regions of the visual and somatomotor networks.
source: To be thorough, we ran the same set of analyses we performed in the DMN (Figures 2–3) in regions of the visual and somatomotor networks extracted from the same atlas parcellation (Schaefer et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed in the study.

claim: The results revealed larger overall differences in DMN than in visual and somatosensory networks for the key comparisons.
source: Our results revealed larger overall differences in DMN than in visual and somatosensory networks for the key comparisons discussed previously (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the additional analysis.

claim: The only regions showing significant differences in pISC in recall-recall and encoding-recall comparisons (p<0.01, uncorrected) were located in the DMN.
source: In particular, the only regions showing significant differences in pISC in recall-recall and encoding-recall comparisons (p<0.01, uncorrected) were located in the DMN.
evidence: This is a finding from the additional analysis.

claim: In the encoding-encoding comparison, several ROIs from the visual and somatomotor networks showed relatively strong effects as well.
source: In the encoding-encoding comparison, several ROIs from the visual and somatomotor networks showed relatively strong effects as well (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the additional analysis.

claim: An ROI-based whole brain analysis qualitatively reproduced the results.
source: In addition, we qualitatively reproduced our results by performing an ROI-based whole brain analysis (Appendix 1—figure 3, p<0.01 uncorrected).
evidence: This describes an additional analysis performed in the study.

claim: The whole brain analysis confirmed the importance of DMN regions for updating neural event representations.
source: This analysis confirmed the importance of DMN regions for updating neural event representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the whole brain analysis.

claim: Strong differences in pISC in the hypothesized direction were also observed in a handful of other non-DMN regions, including ROIs partly overlapping with anterior cingulate cortex and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: However, strong differences in pISC in the hypothesized direction were also observed in a handful of other non-DMN regions, including ROIs partly overlapping with anterior cingulate cortex and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a finding from the whole brain analysis.

claim: At encoding, a widespread network of frontal, parietal, and temporal regions exhibited significantly higher pattern similarity between groups in which participants had the same interpretation of the movie (naive to the twist).
source: At encoding, a widespread network of frontal, parietal, and temporal regions exhibited significantly higher pattern similarity between groups in which participants had the same interpretation of the movie (naive to the twist; see Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a summary of the encoding phase results, shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A belief about the identity of the doctor can shape the encoding processes of new information (the same movie) into memory.
source: This result demonstrates how a belief about the identity of the doctor (which can broadly be construed as the context or the state of mind of the observer) can shape the encoding processes of new information (the same movie) into memory.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the encoding phase results.

claim: Stored representations must be amenable to change as the context changes at a later stage.
source: But information is not only shaped by context during encoding, as stored representations must also be amenable to change as the context changes at a later stage.
evidence: This is a general statement about memory processes.

claim: The neural patterns during recall changed in the twist condition to better match the neural patterns in the spoiled condition observed during recall in the ventromedial PFC, right precuneus, and temporal cortex.
source: In particular, the neural patterns during recall changed in the twist condition to better match the neural patterns in the spoiled condition observed during recall in the ventromedial PFC, right precuneus, and temporal cortex (see Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a summary of the recall phase results, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Numerous areas throughout the DMN showed a significant interaction whereby neural patterns in the 'twist' group became relatively more similar to patterns from the 'spoiled' Ghost group (compared to the 'no-twist' Doctor group) at recall (compared to encoding).
source: Furthermore, numerous areas throughout the DMN showed a significant interaction whereby neural patterns in the 'twist' group became relatively more similar to patterns from the 'spoiled' Ghost group (compared to the 'no-twist' Doctor group) at recall (compared to encoding; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a summary of the interaction analysis results, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Evidence for memory updating was found by directly comparing patterns from encoding and retrieval.
source: We also found evidence for memory updating by directly comparing patterns from encoding and retrieval.
evidence: This is a summary of the encoding-recall analysis results.

claim: In the left angular gyrus, left dorsomedial PFC, and right middle temporal cortex, viewing the twist at the end of the movie (vs. not viewing the twist) resulted in neural patterns at recall becoming more similar to the 'spoiled' Ghost encoding patterns.
source: In the left angular gyrus, left dorsomedial PFC, and right middle temporal cortex, viewing the twist at the end of the movie (vs. not viewing the twist) resulted in neural patterns at recall becoming more similar to the 'spoiled' Ghost encoding patterns (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a summary of the encoding-recall analysis results, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In some regions, the updating effect led to 'twist' recall patterns being numerically more similar to the 'spoiled' encoding patterns than to encoding patterns from the 'twist' condition, but this effect did not survive multiple comparisons correction.
source: In some regions, this updating effect led to 'twist' recall patterns being numerically more similar to the 'spoiled' encoding patterns than to encoding patterns from the 'twist' condition, but this effect did not survive multiple comparisons correction (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a summary of the encoding-recall analysis results, shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The weakness of the effect may be attributable to some participants not fully discarding the Doctor interpretation when they update their interpretation.
source: We suggested that the weakness of this effect may be attributable to some participants not fully discarding the Doctor interpretation when they update their interpretation; in line with this, an exploratory analysis showed that—in some DMN ROIs—the degree of neural change was nominally correlated (across participants) with behavioral 'twist scores' capturing how strongly a participant's recall was influenced by the twist (Appendix 1—figure 1; these exploratory correlations did not survive multiple comparisons correction).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the weak effects observed.

claim: The results provide further evidence for the involvement of DMN regions in integrating new information with prior knowledge to form distinct high-level event representations.
source: Taken together, our results provide further evidence for the involvement of DMN regions in integrating new information with prior knowledge to form distinct high-level event representations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: A subset of core DMN regions are implicated in representing changes in event interpretations during memory updating.
source: In particular, we suggest a subset of core DMN regions are implicated in representing changes in event interpretations during memory updating.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The default mode network is now considered a major hub for actively processing incoming external information and integrating it with prior knowledge in the social world.
source: The default mode network, traditionally known to support internally oriented processes, is now considered a major hub for actively processing incoming external information and integrating it with prior knowledge in the social world (Yeshurun et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: There have been many studies corroborating the discovery of a cortical hierarchy of increasing temporal receptive windows where high-level event representations are encoded at the top of the hierarchy—in the DMN.
source: There have been many studies to date corroborating the discovery of a cortical hierarchy of increasing temporal receptive windows where high-level event representations are encoded at the top of the hierarchy—in the DMN (Hasson et al., 2008; Lerner et al., 2011; Hasson et al., 2015; Baldassano et al., 2018; etc).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DMN is involved in episodic encoding and retrieval.
source: This network is involved in episodic encoding and retrieval (Rugg and Vilberg, 2013) and constructive memory-related tasks such as imagining fictitious scenes and future events (Addis et al., 2007; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Hassabis and Maguire, 2007; Rugg and Vilberg, 2013; Schacter and Addis, 2007; Schacter and Addis, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The design relies on an event-level correspondence between the encoding (viewing) and verbal recall of movie scenes.
source: Our design relies on an event-level correspondence between the encoding (viewing) and verbal recall of movie scenes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Previous research has localized modality-independent representations of movie scenes and their similarity during encoding and recall to the DMN.
source: Previous research has localized modality-independent representations of movie scenes (Zadbood et al., 2017) and their similarity during encoding and recall (Chen et al., 2017) to the DMN.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The DMN is a good candidate to contribute to memory updating—a constructive process in which new information is integrated into past event memories in service of better guiding behavior.
source: These characteristics make this network a good candidate to contribute to memory updating—a constructive process in which new information is integrated into past event memories in service of better guiding behavior.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from prior research and the current study's design.

claim: The findings support the idea that the DMN contributes to memory updating by showing the shift in neural representations during updated recall in a subset of regions in this network.
source: Our findings support this idea by showing the shift in neural representations during updated recall in a subset of regions in this network.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: At encoding, a widespread set of areas including dorsal and lateral PFC, left precuneus, left retrosplenial cortex, and left angular gyrus had differentiable neural patterns across the two interpretations of the movie.
source: At encoding, a widespread set of areas including dorsal and lateral PFC, left precuneus, left retrosplenial cortex, and left angular gyrus had differentiable neural patterns across the two interpretations of the movie.
evidence: This is a summary of the encoding phase results.

claim: These results are consistent with previous work that showed the time course of brain responses in DMN distinguishes between groups when participants are prompted to take two different perspectives before listening to an audio story.
source: These results are consistent with previous work that showed the time course of brain responses in DMN distinguishes between groups when participants are prompted to take two different perspectives before listening to an audio story (Yeshurun et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The results extend previous findings to an audiovisual movie, and provide evidence that interpretative perspective is also encoded in spatially distributed neural response patterns for narrative events, averaged across minutes-long scenes.
source: We extend these results to an audiovisual movie, and provide evidence that interpretative perspective is also encoded in spatially distributed neural response patterns for narrative events, averaged across minutes-long scenes.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The difference in neural responses measured by Yeshurun and colleagues was not significant between the two perspectives of the story in the ventral portion of mPFC.
source: Interestingly, the difference in neural responses measured by Yeshurun and colleagues was not significant between the two perspectives of the story in the ventral portion of mPFC.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: vmPFC ROIs did not exhibit a significant difference between the Doctor and Ghost representations during the encoding phase in the current experiment.
source: Similarly, vmPFC ROIs did not exhibit a significant difference between the Doctor and Ghost representations during the encoding phase in our experiment.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Previous research has implicated mPFC in processing schematic information and integration of new information into prior knowledge.
source: Previous research has implicated mPFC in processing schematic information and integration of new information into prior knowledge (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Schlichting and Preston, 2017; van Kesteren et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Using naturalistic clips as schematic events, it has been shown that response patterns in mPFC are particularly dependent on intact and predictable schemas.
source: Using naturalistic clips as schematic events, it has been shown that response patterns in mPFC are particularly dependent on intact and predictable schemas (Baldassano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The manipulation (Doctor and Ghost interpretations) may not have substantially altered the schemas that participants were using during movie-viewing.
source: Together, these results suggest that our manipulation (Doctor and Ghost interpretations) may not have substantially altered the schemas that participants were using during movie-viewing (e.g. during a restaurant scene, participants will need to use their 'restaurant' schema to interpret it, regardless of whether the doctor is alive or a ghost)—although we interpret these null results with caution.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the null results in vmPFC during encoding.

claim: Groups had different knowledge/perspectives during encoding, but higher pattern similarity across groups if they had similar twist knowledge during recall in vmPFC, right precuneus, and parts of temporal cortex.
source: Even though groups had different knowledge/perspectives during encoding, we found higher pattern similarity across groups if they had similar twist knowledge during recall in vmPFC, right precuneus, and parts of temporal cortex.
evidence: This is a summary of the recall phase results.

claim: Previous findings suggest mPFC is involved in not just encoding but retrieval of memories in relation to prior knowledge and retrieval of overlapping representations to support integration and organization of related memories.
source: Previous findings suggest mPFC is involved in not just encoding but retrieval of memories in relation to prior knowledge (Brod et al., 2015; van Kesteren et al., 2010) and retrieval of overlapping representations to support integration and organization of related memories (Tompary and Davachi, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The observations during recall fit with previous findings and suggest that shifting toward a more similar perspective during recall leads to higher neural similarity in mPFC.
source: Our observations during recall fit with these findings and suggest that shifting toward a more similar perspective during recall leads to higher neural similarity in mPFC.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and prior research.

claim: During encoding, there was no significant pattern correlation between groups that held the same interpretation of the movie in vmPFC.
source: However, during encoding, we did not observe a significant pattern correlation between groups that held the same interpretation of the movie.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: vmPFC was significant in the interaction analysis, indicating that the similarity structure of vmPFC patterns across conditions was significantly different at encoding versus retrieval.
source: Furthermore, vmPFC was significant in our interaction analysis (Figure 2C), indicating that the similarity structure of vmPFC patterns across conditions was significantly different at encoding versus retrieval.
evidence: This is a finding from the study, shown in Figure 2C.

claim: These results suggest vmPFC is differently implicated in encoding and recall of story-specific representations during processing of naturalistic events.
source: Together, these results suggest vmPFC is differently implicated in encoding and recall of story-specific representations during processing of naturalistic events.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Precuneus is a core region in the posterior medial network, which is hypothesized to be involved in constructing and applying situation models.
source: Precuneus is a core region in the posterior medial network, which is hypothesized to be involved in constructing and applying situation models (Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The findings support a role for precuneus in deploying interpretation-specific situation models when retrieving event memories.
source: Our findings support a role for precuneus in deploying interpretation-specific situation models when retrieving event memories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The posterior medial network may encode a shift in the situation model of the 'twist' group in order to accommodate the new Ghost interpretation.
source: In particular, we suggest that the posterior medial network may encode a shift in the situation model of the 'twist' group in order to accommodate the new Ghost interpretation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Two targeted analyses were performed to look for evidence of memory updating across encoding and recall: the interaction analysis and the encoding-recall analysis.
source: We performed two targeted analyses to look for evidence of memory updating across encoding and recall: the interaction analysis (Figure 2C) and the encoding-recall analysis (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: A shift in direction of pISC difference would occur when neural representations during recall in the 'twist' group start to reflect the Ghost interpretation.
source: We hypothesized that a shift in direction of pISC difference would occur when neural representations during recall in the 'twist' group start to reflect the Ghost interpretation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis of the study.

claim: The interaction analysis probed the shift indirectly by taking into account the effects of both encoding-encoding and recall-recall analyses.
source: The interaction analysis probed this shift indirectly by taking into account the effects of both encoding-encoding and recall-recall analyses.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: In the encoding-recall analysis, neural event representations during encoding and recall were directly compared.
source: Unlike the interaction analysis, in the encoding-recall analysis, we directly compared neural event representations during encoding and recall.
evidence: This describes the analysis approach used in the study.

claim: All regions exhibiting an effect across the two encoding-recall analyses, excluding left anterior temporal cortex, were present in the interaction results.
source: Interestingly, all regions exhibiting an effect across the two encoding-recall analyses, excluding left anterior temporal cortex, were present in the interaction results.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the different analyses.

claim: The left angular gyrus/TPJ exhibited an effect across all three analyses (interaction, encoding-recall).
source: Among these regions, the left angular gyrus/TPJ exhibited an effect across all three analyses.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the different analyses.

claim: As a core hub in the mentalizing network, temporo-parietal cortex has been implicated in theory of mind through perspective-taking, rationalizing the mental state of someone else, and modeling the attentional state of others.
source: As a core hub in the mentalizing network, temporo-parietal cortex has been implicated in theory of mind through perspective-taking, rationalizing the mental state of someone else, and modeling the attentional state of others (Frith and Frith, 2006; Guterstam et al., 2021; Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The motivations behind some actions of the main character in the movie heavily depend on whether the viewer perceives them as a Doctor or a Ghost, and participants may focus on this during both encoding and recall.
source: The motivations behind some actions of the main character in the movie heavily depend on whether the viewer perceives them as a Doctor or a Ghost, and participants may focus on this during both encoding and recall.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the movie content.

claim: Neural event representations in AG/TPJ in the current experiment may be related to mentalizing about the main character's actions.
source: We speculate that neural event representations in AG/TPJ in the current experiment may be related to mentalizing about the main character's actions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural findings.

claim: The updated event representations during recall following the twist would be more closely aligned to the 'spoiled' encoding representations, as a consequence of memory updating in the 'twist' group.
source: Under this interpretation, the updated event representations during recall following the twist would be more closely aligned to the 'spoiled' encoding representations, as a consequence of memory updating in the 'twist' group.
evidence: This is a speculation about the neural findings.

claim: The findings are consistent with the view that DMN synthesizes incoming information with one's prior beliefs and memories.
source: Our findings are consistent with the view that DMN synthesizes incoming information with one's prior beliefs and memories (Yeshurun et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings and prior research.

claim: The study adds to the framework by providing evidence for the involvement of DMN regions in updating prior beliefs in light of new knowledge.
source: We add to this framework by providing evidence for the involvement of DMN regions in updating prior beliefs in light of new knowledge.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Memory updating effects are observed in a varied subset of DMN regions that do not cleanly map onto a specific subsystem of DMN.
source: Across our different encoding and recall analyses, we observe memory updating effects in a varied subset of DMN regions that do not cleanly map onto a specific subsystem of DMN (Robin and Moscovitch, 2017; Ranganath and Ritchey, 2012; Ritchey and Cooper, 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The results might be reflecting inherent differences between the processes of encoding and recall of naturalistic events.
source: Rather than being divergent, these results might be reflecting inherent differences between the processes of encoding and recall of naturalistic events.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the varied results across analyses.

claim: It has been proposed that neural representations corresponding to encoding of events are systematically transformed during recall of those events.
source: It has been proposed that neural representations corresponding to encoding of events are systematically transformed during recall of those events (Chen et al., 2017; Favila et al., 2020; Musz and Chen, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The study provides evidence for reinstatement of memories in DMN.
source: While we provide evidence for reinstatement of memories in DMN, our findings also support a transformation of neural representation during recall, as encoding-recall results were weaker in some areas than recall-recall findings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: The findings support a transformation of neural representation during recall, as encoding-recall results were weaker in some areas than recall-recall findings.
source: While we provide evidence for reinstatement of memories in DMN, our findings also support a transformation of neural representation during recall, as encoding-recall results were weaker in some areas than recall-recall findings.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: This transformation could affect how different regions and sub-systems of DMN represent memories.
source: This transformation could affect how different regions and sub-systems of DMN represent memories, and suggests that the concerted activity of multiple subsystems and neural mechanisms might be at play during encoding, recall and successful updating of naturalistic event memories.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: The concerted activity of multiple subsystems and neural mechanisms might be at play during encoding, recall and successful updating of naturalistic event memories.
source: This transformation could affect how different regions and sub-systems of DMN represent memories, and suggests that the concerted activity of multiple subsystems and neural mechanisms might be at play during encoding, recall and successful updating of naturalistic event memories.
evidence: This is a speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: The effects observed during encoding-encoding analysis in sensory regions could reflect similarity in perception of the movie guided by similar attentional state while watching scenes with the same interpretation.
source: Therefore, the effects observed during encoding-encoding analysis in sensory regions could reflect similarity in perception of the movie guided by similar attentional state while watching scenes with the same interpretation (e.g. similarity in gaze location, paying attention to certain dialogues, or small body movements while watching the movie with the same Doctor or Ghost interpretations).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in sensory regions.

claim: In the whole-brain analysis, sensory regions did not have significant interaction effects, which suggests that the effects were isolated to encoding.
source: In our whole brain analysis, these regions did not have significant interaction effects, which suggests that the effects were isolated to encoding.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole brain analysis.

claim: In the whole-brain analysis, a significant encoding-encoding and interaction effects were observed in anterior cingulate cortex, as well as recall-recall and interaction effects in dlPFC.
source: In the whole-brain analysis, we also observed a significant encoding-encoding and interaction effects in anterior cingulate cortex, as well as recall-recall and interaction effects in dlPFC.
evidence: This is a finding from the whole brain analysis.

claim: Both the 'spoiled' manipulation and the 'twist' may recruit top-down control and conflict monitoring processes during naturalistic viewing and recall.
source: These results suggest that both the 'spoiled' manipulation and the 'twist' may recruit top-down control and conflict monitoring processes during naturalistic viewing and recall.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in ACC and dlPFC.

claim: The findings provide further insight into the functional role of the DMN.
source: Our findings provide further insight into the functional role of the DMN.
evidence: This is a general statement about the study's contribution.

claim: These results have been obtained using only one movie.
source: However, these results have been obtained using only one movie.
evidence: This is a limitation of the study.

claim: Naturalistic paradigms better capture the complexity of real life and provide greater ecological generalizability than highly-controlled experimental stimuli and tasks.
source: While naturalistic paradigms better capture the complexity of real life and provide greater ecological generalizability than highly-controlled experimental stimuli and tasks (Nastase et al., 2020), they are still limited by the properties of the particular naturalistic stimulus used.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Naturalistic paradigms are still limited by the properties of the particular naturalistic stimulus used.
source: While naturalistic paradigms better capture the complexity of real life and provide greater ecological generalizability than highly-controlled experimental stimuli and tasks (Nastase et al., 2020), they are still limited by the properties of the particular naturalistic stimulus used.
evidence: This is a limitation of naturalistic paradigms.

claim: This movie—including the twist itself—hinges on suspension of disbelief about the existence of ghosts.
source: For example, this movie—including the twist itself—hinges on suspension of disbelief about the existence of ghosts.
evidence: This is a characteristic of the stimulus used.

claim: Future work is needed to extend the findings about updating event memories to a broader class of naturalistic stimuli.
source: Future work is needed to extend our findings about updating event memories to a broader class of naturalistic stimuli: for example, movies with different kinds of (non-supernatural) plot twists, spoken stories with twist endings, or using autobiographical real-life situations where new information (e.g. discovering a longtime friend has lied about something important) triggers re-evaluation of the past (e.g. reinterpreting their friend's previous actions).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: The current method relies on averaging spatially coarse activity patterns across subjects (and time points within an event).
source: Moreover, our current method relies on averaging spatially coarse activity patterns across subjects (and time points within an event).
evidence: This is a limitation of the current method.

claim: Future extensions of this work may benefit from using functional alignment methods to capture more fine-grained event representations which are shared across participants.
source: Future extensions of this work may benefit from using functional alignment methods (Haxby et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2015) to capture more fine-grained event representations which are shared across participants.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: During recall, many participants recounted both the old and new interpretations (Ghost and Doctor) of movie scenes.
source: During recall, many participants recounted both the old and new interpretations (Ghost and Doctor) of movie scenes.
evidence: This is a behavioral observation from the study.

claim: This behavior indicated that participants maintained both representations in parallel (possibly competing), rather than overwriting the old representation with new information.
source: This behavior indicated that they maintained both representations in parallel (possibly competing), rather than overwriting the old representation with new information.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the behavioral data.

claim: The simultaneous presence of these representations poses an interesting theoretical question for future studies: When does updating the memory cause us to lose traces of the old interpretation, and when do the old and new interpretations end up co-existing in memory?
source: The simultaneous presence of these representations poses an interesting theoretical question for future studies: When does updating the memory cause us to lose traces of the old interpretation, and when do the old and new interpretations end up co-existing in memory?
evidence: This is a question for future research.

claim: Previous studies have shown that old and new memory traces are simultaneously reactivated in the brain, leading to competition.
source: Previous studies have shown that old and new memory traces are simultaneously reactivated in the brain, leading to competition (e.g. Kuhl et al., 2012), and this competition can trigger learning processes that resolve the competition; for example, by weakening one of the memories or by restructuring the memories so they can coexist (Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Competition between old and new memory traces can trigger learning processes that resolve the competition; for example, by weakening one of the memories or by restructuring the memories so they can coexist.
source: Previous studies have shown that old and new memory traces are simultaneously reactivated in the brain, leading to competition (e.g. Kuhl et al., 2012), and this competition can trigger learning processes that resolve the competition; for example, by weakening one of the memories or by restructuring the memories so they can coexist (Ritvo et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Understanding how competition between interpretations plays out over time is an important topic for future work.
source: Understanding how competition between interpretations plays out over time is an important topic for future work; existing research on memory revaluation suggests that updating may be a temporally-extended process driven by successive replays of the new information, rather than taking place all at once (see, e.g., Momennejad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a suggestion for future research.

claim: Existing research on memory revaluation suggests that updating may be a temporally-extended process driven by successive replays of the new information, rather than taking place all at once.
source: Understanding how competition between interpretations plays out over time is an important topic for future work; existing research on memory revaluation suggests that updating may be a temporally-extended process driven by successive replays of the new information, rather than taking place all at once (see, e.g., Momennejad et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In clinical settings, methods inspired by reconsolidation and memory updating are extensively used to treat maladaptive memories.
source: In clinical settings, methods inspired by reconsolidation and memory updating are extensively used to treat maladaptive memories (Phelps and Hofmann, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: In clinical contexts, it will be especially important to understand the factors that influence the 'end state' of this competition between interpretations.
